name: Ad click IDs (gclid, fbclid, msclkid and more)
plain: Unique IDs ad platforms add to links so a later purchase can be matched to the exact ad click.
meaning: A click ID ties one person's click on an ad to later conversions, even across sessions, and is stored in a first-party cookie (for example Google _gcl_aw about 90 days, Meta _fbc about 90 days). iOS ATT era gbraid/wbraid are aggregated.

web.api: URL query: gclid, gbraid, wbraid (Google), fbclid (Meta), msclkid (Microsoft), ttclid (TikTok), li_fat_id (LinkedIn), twclid (X), epik (Pinterest), igshid (Instagram)

access.persistence: First-party cookie copies, typically 30 to 90 days, then sent to ad platforms via pixel or server API

limits.headline: Can tag your ad click so a later purchase links back to that exact ad
limits.user_action: You click an ad link that carries a code such as gclid, fbclid or msclkid
can: Add a unique code to the web address of the page you land on
Let the site or its ad tools save that code
Match a later purchase or sign up to your ad click
Pass the code to the ad company on the server side
cannot: Exist unless you arrived through an ad link with the code
Follow you to other sites on its own
Work if your browser strips known codes from links, in some modes
Name you; it is a code, not a name, until matched to an account
limits.differs: Safari, Firefox and Brave remove some of these codes from links in certain modes. Chrome keeps them.

story.what_it_is: A unique code added to an ad link so a later purchase can be matched to that exact click.

marketing.name: Link Tracking Protection
marketing.pitch: Apple says Safari 17 removes tracking codes from links in Private Browsing, Mail and Messages to protect privacy.

story.for_you: You click an ad and the web address ends in a long string of letters and numbers. You may not notice it. The site saves that code, so a sale next week can be tied to your click.
story.for_makers: Advertisers want to know which ad paid off, down to one click. A click code stored in the advertiser's own cookie survives most privacy rules for about three months. It is the base of nearly all ad accounting, and the reason for the arms race with browser protections.

use_cases.example: You click a Google ad for running shoes. A gclid is added, the shop stores it, and the sale is credited to that click.
You tap an Instagram ad, an fbclid joins the link, and Meta can link your purchase to that ad.
A mobile game web store tracks which ad brought a player who later buys gems, to pay the ad network.
A marketer sees which of 40 ads made money, instead of only which got clicks.
A retailer in a Black Friday ad run sees which keyword made the sale and moves budget in real time.
Fraud teams look for the same click code used by many sales, which is a sign of fake traffic.
A newsletter site sees which ad created each paying subscriber, and which only brought free readers.

risks: Ties a click to a person
Codes can leak in shared links

technical_bounds: Stripped in Safari Private Browsing, Mail and Messages (Link Tracking Protection) and Firefox ETP Strict
Platforms may refuse conversions older than their attribution window (often 7 to 90 days)
Only identifies a click, not a person's identity by itself

abuse: Sharing click ID with unrelated vendors

history.change: Link Tracking Protection strips known click IDs in Private Browsing, Mail and Messages
Query Parameter Stripping removes known trackers in ETP Strict and Private windows
